reports.title: USA Sweeps Gold at 2026 Bass Fishing World Championship
reports.text:
Host Team USA took home the win at the 20th Black Bass Fishing World Championship on Lake Hamilton, Arkansas, completing a dominant performance across three days of fishing. Legendary bass angler Kevin VanDam and teammate three-time Redcrest Champion Dustin Connell captured the individual pair title.
The United States finished atop the team standings (133 pounds, 5 ounces) after three demanding days from October 1 through October 3, holding off silver medalist South Africa (100 pounds) and third-place finisher France (90 pounds, 2 ounces). reports.text:

reports.text:

They start finding moderate success on a certain lure and think, “I could make this bait even better.” And then they start tinkering.
That’s how some of the greatest fishing lures of our time were invented. Let’s dive in and take a look.

by Madalyn Roberts

Crappie Basics: Match the Hatch for More Crappie

One of the simplest ways to improve your crappie fishing is to give the fish what they’re already looking for. That means matching your jig to the size and general shape of the forage crappie are feeding on.
If 2-inch minnows make up a big part of the crappie diet in the lake you’re fishing, for example, a 2-inch jig is a logical choice. S hane Walser of Yadkin Lakes Crappie Guides (336-978-3737) loves fishing High Rock Lake in October.
“It’s a great time to fish, for numerous reasons. The weather is ideal, the summer lake crowds are gone, and the crappie really pick up the bite with the falling temperatures,” he said.

reports.title: Yeopim Creek Fliers with Carolina ALL OUT
reports.text:
Fliers are among the most unique panfish in the Carolinas
T he Carolinas are full of numerous species of panfish, and for their size, they all fight like champs. They’re also very tasty. Fliers, although they are found throughout the southeast, are among the least widely distributed panfish, mostly living in swampy, acidic blackwater creeks with low pH.
Where you’ll find fliers, you can always count on finding other panfish as well. They overlap with crappie, bluegill, redbreast and shellcrackers, among other species.

reports.title: How To: Hot Summertime Tactics for catching crappie
reports.text:
Hot Summertime Tactics for Catching Crappie
When summer water gets hot, crappie usually leave the shallow cover and seek cooler, more oxygenated water, shade, and baitfish. The key is finding where those conditions overlap.
Fish deeper: Start around 15–30 feet, then adjust based on your lake’s depth and thermocline. Electronics are extremely helpful for locating suspended schools.
Target brush piles: Deep brush, submerged trees, and man-made structure can hold crappie throughout summer. Slowly work a jig vertically around the cover.
Follow the bait: Find schools of shad or other forage and look nearby—and often directly beneath them—for crappie.

Northland’s underspin jig, the Deep Vee Spin, is a catcher. Cast it or troll it and you’ll catch fish. This jig shines in crystal clear waters where its flashy willow blade makes all the difference in getting fish’s attention and getting bit. The jig has a keeled body shape to help it fall fast and track straight. Built into the design is a wire keeper that ensures plastics stay snug on the hook shank.
